steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on early object detection, where small distant objects are hard to detect, proposing to refine only the image patches that contain objects with a conditional diffusion model. Explain the problem, why super-resolution helps but is costly, our method, and list our contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Object detection (OD) plays a vital role in many real-world applications, such as autonomous driving and robotics. There are many different algorithms for this task, but existing methods still have big challenges in early object detection, which is crucial because it enables prompt and proactive decision-making. In these scenarios the objects in captured images are often much smaller because of long distances. As shown in Fig. 1, when images contain only a limited number of objects, the performance of object detection gets much worse due to insufficient data volume.

To address this challenge we can use super-resolution (SR) algorithms to reconstruct higher-resolution images, which augments the data available for the object detection models that come after. SR is also a classic problem in computer vision and there are lots of solutions made for it. Recently diffusion models, such as DDPM, have shown remarkable capabilities in image generation and are more stable than generative adversarial networks (GAN). Also, research on applying Conditional Diffusion Models (CDM) for SR has made notable advancements. By using diffusion models to generate high-resolution images we can get substantial improvements in object detection performance, especially for datasets where the object-to-image ratio is low. However, diffusion models have a significant computational cost, which is a challenge for real-world applications like autonomous driving. In the image example in Fig. 1, refining the whole image puts a considerable computational burden on background pixels, and this is an excessive waste of resources that does not contribute anything meaningful to OD.

- DPR
  - CDM reconstructs only patches containing objects; Patch-Selector module classifies patches
  - localizing small objects directly is hard; deciding presence of objects in a patch is more feasible
  - filter irrelevant patches -> less data -> immediate CDM refinement -> better OD accuracy
  - hierarchical patch encoder inspired by Swin Transformer
  - patch classifier via classification token, like ViT
  - pyramid patch class label for enough positive patches
  - experiments on BDD100K
- Contributions
  - Patch-Selector with attention; hierarchical architecture + pyramid loss
  - CDM refines only selected patches
  - negative patches enlarged by interpolation, combined into complete images; competitive early OD, 77.2% less computation

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Object detection (OD) plays a vital role in many real-world applications, such as autonomous driving and robotics. There are many different algorithms for this task, but existing methods still have big challenges in early object detection, which is crucial because it enables prompt and proactive decision-making. In these scenarios the objects in captured images are often much smaller because of long distances. As shown in Fig. 1, when images contain only a limited number of objects, the performance of object detection gets much worse due to insufficient data volume.

To address this challenge we can use super-resolution (SR) algorithms to reconstruct higher-resolution images, which augments the data available for the object detection models that come after. SR is also a classic problem in computer vision and there are lots of solutions made for it. Recently diffusion models, such as DDPM, have shown remarkable capabilities in image generation and are more stable than generative adversarial networks (GAN). Also, research on applying Conditional Diffusion Models (CDM) for SR has made notable advancements. By using diffusion models to generate high-resolution images we can get substantial improvements in object detection performance, especially for datasets where the object-to-image ratio is low. However, diffusion models have a significant computational cost, which is a challenge for real-world applications like autonomous driving. In the image example in Fig. 1, refining the whole image puts a considerable computational burden on background pixels, and this is an excessive waste of resources that does not contribute anything meaningful to OD.

In this paper we introduce a new algorithm called Dichotomized Patch Refinement (DPR) to tackle this problem. DPR uses CDM to reconstruct only the patches that contain objects, and it uses a Patch-Selector module to classify patches accurately. Directly localizing small objects is quite challenging, but deciding whether there are objects in a patch or not is a more feasible approach. With the Patch-Selector module we can efficiently filter out the irrelevant patches that do not contribute to the OD task afterwards. This strategy reduces the data volume a lot, which lets us immediately generate refined images with CDM and greatly improve object detection accuracy. To implement the module, we design a hierarchical patch encoder inspired by the structure of the Swin Transformer to extract embeddings for the individual patches. We also add a patch classifier by introducing a classification token, similar to the approach in ViT. In addition, following the hierarchical structure of our network, we introduce a pyramid patch class label so that enough positive patches are included. Our experiments on the BDD100K dataset give strong evidence of DPR's efficacy and accuracy for early object detection.

Our key contributions are:

- We design a Patch-Selector module that uses the attention mechanism to sift out the patches that contain objects from images. We also introduce a hierarchical architecture and use a pyramid loss function to make the selection better.

- Using Conditional Diffusion Models (CDM), we refine only the selected patches, which gives better object detection performance.

- We enlarge negative patches with interpolation and combine all the processed patches into complete images. With comprehensive experiments on both patches and entire images we show that DPR gets competitive early object detection performance with 77.2% reduction of the computation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Object detection (OD) plays a vital role in numerous real-world applications, such as autonomous driving and robotics. Despite the proliferation of diverse algorithms for this task, existing methods still face significant challenges in early object detection, which is crucial for enabling prompt and proactive decision-making. In such scenarios, objects in captured images are often significantly reduced in size due to long distances. As illustrated in Fig. 1, when images contain only a limited number of objects, the performance of object detection significantly deteriorates due to insufficient data volume.

To address this challenge, we can exploit super-resolution (SR) algorithms to reconstruct higher-resolution images, thereby augmenting the data available for subsequent object detection models. SR is itself a classic problem in computer vision, with a plethora of solutions tailored for it. Recently, diffusion models such as DDPM [1] have shown remarkable capabilities in image generation and greater stability than generative adversarial networks (GAN) [2]. Moreover, research on applying Conditional Diffusion Models (CDM) [3,4] to SR has yielded notable advancements. By using diffusion models for high-resolution image generation, we can achieve substantial improvements in object detection performance, particularly for datasets with a low object-to-image ratio. However, diffusion models come with a significant computational cost, which poses a challenge for real-world applications like autonomous driving. As the image example in Fig. 1 shows, refining the whole image places a considerable computational burden on background pixels, an excessive waste of resources that makes no meaningful contribution to OD.

In this paper, we introduce a novel algorithm, named Dichotomized Patch Refinement (DPR), to tackle this problem. DPR leverages CDM to reconstruct only the patches that contain objects, employing a Patch-Selector module for accurate patch classification. While directly localizing small objects is very challenging, discerning whether objects are present within patches is a more feasible approach. With the Patch-Selector module, we can efficiently filter out irrelevant patches that do not contribute to the subsequent OD task. This strategy significantly reduces the data volume, enabling the immediate generation of refined images using CDM to greatly enhance object detection accuracy. To implement the module, we devise a hierarchical patch encoder inspired by the structure of the Swin Transformer [5] to extract embeddings for individual patches. Furthermore, we incorporate a patch classifier by introducing a classification token, following an approach similar to ViT [6]. In line with our network's hierarchical structure, we also introduce a pyramid patch class label to ensure that enough positive patches are included. Our experiments on the BDD100K dataset provide compelling evidence of DPR's efficacy and accuracy for early object detection.

To summarize, our key contributions are as follows:

- We design a Patch-Selector module, incorporating the attention mechanism, to effectively sift patches containing objects from images. We also introduce a hierarchical architecture and employ a pyramid loss function to further improve the selection.

- By harnessing Conditional Diffusion Models (CDM), we refine only the selected patches, yielding enhanced object detection performance.

- By enlarging negative patches with interpolation, we combine all processed patches into complete images. Through comprehensive experiments on both patches and entire images, we demonstrate that DPR achieves competitive early object detection performance with 77.2% reduction of the computation.

References:
[1] Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain, and Pieter Abbeel. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems , 33:6840–6851, 2020.
[2] Ian Goodfellow, Jean Pouget-Abadie, Mehdi Mirza, Bing Xu, David Warde-Farley, Sherjil Ozair, Aaron Courville, and Yoshua Bengio. Generative adversarial networks. Communications of the ACM , 63(11):139–144, 2020.
[3] Chitwan Saharia, Jonathan Ho, William Chan, Tim Salimans, David J Fleet, and Mohammad Norouzi. Image super-resolution via iterative refinement. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence , 2022.
[4] Jonathan Ho, Chitwan Saharia, William Chan, David J Fleet, Mohammad Norouzi, and Tim Salimans. Cascaded diffusion models for high fidelity image generation. J. Mach. Learn. Res. , 23(47):1–33, 2022.
[5] Ze Liu, Yutong Lin, Yue Cao, Han Hu, Yixuan Wei, Zheng Zhang, Stephen Lin, and Baining Guo. Swin transformer: Hierarchical vision transformer using shifted windows. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF international conference on computer vision , pages 10012–10022, 2021.
